Posterior predictive check

Source: R/plot-ppc.R
plot_ppc.Rd

plot_ppc() is a graphical posterior predictive check. It compares the estimates with the distribution that the fitted model predicts for them, through the probability integral transform (PIT) of each estimate or through the marginal density of the estimates.

Usage

plot_ppc(
  x,
  type = c("pit_ecdf", "pit_hist", "marginal"),
  loo = FALSE,
  level = 0.95,
  scale = 1,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

A bef_fit object created by bayes_efron_fit().

type

Type of plot: "pit_ecdf" (the default), "pit_hist" or "marginal". See Details.

loo

If TRUE, the PIT of each site is computed from the posterior distribution without that site (leave-one-out). Not used with type = "marginal".

level

Level of the pointwise reference intervals, a number between 0 and 1. Not used with type = "marginal".

scale

Positive number by which the estimates are multiplied on the horizontal axis. Only used with type = "marginal".

...

These dots are for future extensions and must be empty.

Value

A ggplot object.

Details

Under the model, the estimate of a site is an effect from \(g\) plus normal sampling error, so its distribution is \(g\) convolved with a normal distribution whose standard deviation is the site's standard error. The PIT of an estimate is the probability that the model assigns to a smaller estimate at that site. If \(g\) were known and the model were correct, the PIT values would be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, so the check compares the PIT values of the fitted model with the uniform distribution.

For site \(i\) with estimate \(\hat\theta_i\) and standard error \(\sigma_i\), and for one posterior draw of the probabilities \(g_j\) at the grid points \(\tau_j\), $$\mathrm{PIT}_i = \sum_j g_j \, \Phi\left(\frac{\hat\theta_i - \tau_j} {\sqrt{\sigma_i^2 + \tau_c^2}}\right),$$ where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function and \(\tau_c\) is the standard deviation of a normal component (zero for point masses). The plots show the mean of \(\mathrm{PIT}_i\) over the posterior draws.

There are three types of plot.

  • "pit_ecdf" shows the empirical distribution function of the PIT values minus the distribution function of the uniform distribution, with pointwise reference intervals for independent uniform values.

  • "pit_hist" shows a histogram of the PIT values, with the corresponding reference intervals for the height of a bar. If there are fewer than 30 sites, the bars would contain too few values, and the "pit_ecdf" plot is shown instead.

  • "marginal" shows a histogram of the estimates together with the density that the model assigns to an estimate, averaged over the standard errors of the sites.

The reference intervals are computed for independent uniform values, which is what the PIT values would be if \(g\) were known. However, the PIT values of a fitted model all depend on the same estimate of \(g\), and the band ignores this dependence. Its level is therefore not the probability that the line of a fitted model lies inside the band at a given point, with or without loo = TRUE.

Because the model was fitted to the same estimates that it is checked against, the check is lenient. With loo = TRUE, the PIT of each site is computed from the posterior distribution without that site, using Pareto smoothed importance sampling. This requires the loo package.

The check can show that the estimates are not what a normal likelihood with the given standard errors and some \(g\) on this grid would produce, e.g., because the standard errors are too small, the grid is too narrow, or there are too few spline functions. Note that it cannot show that the shape of \(g\) is correct. Distributions of effects with different shapes give nearly the same distribution of noisy estimates, so a model can pass the check with a wrong \(g\).

See also

plot_diagnostics(), loo.bef_fit(), vignette("diagnostics")

Examples

plot_ppc(krw_fit)

plot_ppc(twin_towers_fit, type = "pit_hist")

plot_ppc(krw_fit, type = "marginal", scale = 100)
